title: The problem: mothers still dying
plain_summary: Sub-Saharan Africa has the world's highest risk of dying in pregnancy or childbirth, and Tanzania is among the hardest hit, with surveys putting the death rate near 556 per 100,000 births. Hospital records could show what's killing these women, but they're rarely analysed.

title: What the study did
plain_summary: Researchers pulled ten years of records (2006-2015) from 34 public hospitals across the country - about a third of Tanzania's public hospitals. They took every death of a woman aged 15-49, then used ICD-10 rules to pick out the maternal deaths and classify what caused them.

title: How many, and who
plain_summary: Of 40,052 women aged 15-49 who died in these hospitals, 1,987 (5%) died from pregnancy or childbirth. Half were under 27, and two thirds were aged 20-34. Deaths among teenage mothers fell over the decade.

title: What killed them
plain_summary: Five in six deaths came from direct obstetric causes. Eclampsia led (34%), then obstetric haemorrhage (25%) and sepsis (17%). Anaemia and heart problems were the main indirect causes, and often went hand in hand with bleeding.

title: What changed over ten years
plain_summary: Hospital maternal deaths rose over the decade and the death rate climbed from about 40 to 58 per 100,000 births. Eclampsia and abortion deaths eased slightly, while haemorrhage and cardiovascular deaths rose. Eclampsia killed the youngest women; haemorrhage the oldest.

title: What it means and what to fix
plain_summary: Most of these deaths are preventable with good emergency care for eclampsia, bleeding and infection. Indirect causes like anaemia and heart disease deserve more attention than they get, and hospital records - if used - can point care to where it's needed.
